title: The history of training the back
tagline: From wrestlers' poles and ropes in India to a pressure needle inside a living disc, and the evidence that exercise helps back pain.
intro: People trained their backs long before anyone could explain how. Indian wrestlers climbed ropes and wooden poles, and yoga and the akhara added back-arching poses to daily routines. Anatomists drew the back's muscles, and Borelli worked out that muscles on short levers must pull many times the load. In the twentieth century researchers put sensors inside living spines, estimated the loads in record lifts, and finally tested what really helps a sore back. The answer, again and again: movement and exercise.

eras.summary: Wrestling and pole gymnastics in India, described in texts from the 12th and 13th centuries.

eras.name: Drawing and weighing the back
eras.summary: Anatomists draw the back's muscles and Borelli treats the body as a set of levers.

eras.name: Gyms, Olympics and revival

events.title: Pole exercises in clay
events.text: Pottery from Chandraketugarh, dated to between the 2nd century BCE and the 1st century CE, is cited as an early example of exercises like mallakhamb. The link is an interpretation, so treat it as possible rather than certain.
events.why: Pole climbing and gripping is one of the oldest ways of training the back and arms together.

events.title: Mallakhamb is written down
events.text: The Sanskrit encyclopaedia Manasollasa, written for the Western Chalukya king Someshvara III, has the earliest known literary mention of mallakhamb: exercise on a wrestler's pole.
events.why: Every climb, grip and hold on the pole loads the lats, the trapezius and the spinal muscles.

events.title: A treatise on wrestling
events.text: The Malla Purana, a 13th-century treatise, describes malla-yuddha, the Indian wrestling that later mixed with Persian koshti in the Mughal era to become pehlwani.
events.why: Akhara training built the back for pulling and lifting opponents long before gyms.

events.title: The muscle men of the Fabrica
events.text: Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica showed the body's muscles peeled layer by layer, including the broad sheets and deep columns of the back, drawn from dissections.
events.why: Layers are still how we learn the back: trapezius and lats on top, erector spinae and multifidus underneath.

events.title: The body as a set of levers
events.text: Borelli's De Motu Animalium, published in two volumes in 1680 and 1681 after his death, treated muscles and bones as machines. He saw that muscles pull close to the joints, so they must pull many times the load they move.
events.why: That is why your back muscles pull thousands of newtons in a deadlift: they sit only about 5.5 cm behind the spine.

events.title: Mallakhamb is revived
events.text: Balambhatta Dada Deodhar, a teacher of Peshwa Baji Rao II, brought new life to mallakhamb in the first half of the 19th century.
events.why: Mallakhamb is still a complete pulling and back workout taught in Indian schools and akharas.

events.title: Rope climbing at the first modern Olympics
events.text: Rope climbing was a gymnastics event at the first modern Olympics, on a rope of about 14 m. It came back in 1904, at the 1906 Intercalated Games, in 1924 and for the last time in 1932.
events.why: A rope climb is a pull-up that keeps going: lats, grip and biceps working hand over hand.

events.title: The Great Gama wins in London
events.text: Gama, trained in the pehlwani tradition of dand, baithak and rope climbing, beat Stanislaus Zbyszko and others in London in 1910 and was hailed as a world champion (Rustam-e-Zaman).
events.why: Traditional akhara training, heavy on bodyweight pulling and pushing, built some of the strongest wrestlers of the age.

events.title: Surya Namaskar gets its name
events.who: Bhawanrao Shriniwasrao Pant Pratinidhi, Raja of Aundh
events.text: The Raja of Aundh popularised and named the sequence in the 1920s and described it in his 1928 book The Ten-Point Way to Health. He said it was already a commonplace Marathi tradition. Krishnamacharya later taught it at the Mysore Palace.
events.why: Its cobra and upward-dog poses are back extensions: the erector spinae arch the spine backwards.

events.title: The last Olympic rope climb
events.who: Gymnasts at the Los Angeles Games
events.text: Rope climbing was held at the Olympics for the last time in 1932, on a rope of about 8 m, and then dropped from the programme.
events.why: It lives on in gyms, armed forces training and akharas as a hard pulling exercise.

events.title: Mallakhamb at the Olympics
events.text: Mallakhamb was demonstrated at the 1936 Summer Olympics, introducing the Indian pole to a world audience.
events.why: It showed a training tradition that loads the back through gripping, climbing and holding the body out.

events.title: Listening to the back muscles
events.who: W. F. Floyd and P. H. S. Silver
events.text: Floyd and Silver recorded the electrical activity of the erector spinae in bending and standing. Their study is widely cited for showing that the muscles can fall quiet at full forward bend, when ligaments take over.
events.why: This 'flexion-relaxation' is why a fully rounded back shifts load from muscle to ligament and disc.

events.title: First national mallakhamb championships
events.text: After appearing at the National Gymnastics Championships in Delhi in 1958, mallakhamb held its first national championships in 1962 at Gwalior.
events.why: Competition turned a training tradition into a sport with rules.

events.title: A needle inside a living disc
events.text: Nachemson and Morris published measurements of pressure inside the lower lumbar discs of living people, made with a needle sensor, after a first report in 1963.
events.why: For the first time, the load on a spine could be measured rather than guessed.

events.title: Powerlifting gets a world body
events.text: After a first world powerlifting event at York, Pennsylvania in 1971, delegates founded the International Powerlifting Federation in 1972. The deadlift is one of the sport's three lifts, with the squat and bench press.
events.why: Record deadlifts later gave researchers some of the heaviest spinal loads ever studied.

events.title: The loads in record lifts
events.who: Jacek Cholewicki, Stuart McGill and Robert Norman
events.text: Filming 57 powerlifters at a national championship, the team estimated moments near 1,000 N·m about the lower back and compression on the L4/L5 disc of up to about 17,000 N. The sumo style cut the moment by about 10%.
events.why: Spines adapt to huge loads when trained gradually, and keeping the bar close changes the lever.

events.title: A lifting equation for work
events.text: The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health revised its equation for judging lifting tasks at work, with the distance of the load from the body as one of its factors.
events.why: The closer the load, the smaller the moment on the lower back: the same lesson as the deadlift.

events.title: Disc pressure in daily life
events.text: A pressure sensor in one 70 kg volunteer's L4–L5 disc read 0.1 MPa lying face down, 0.5 MPa standing and 1.1 MPa bent forward. Lifting 20 kg gave 2.3 MPa with a round back, 1.7 MPa with bent knees and 1.1 MPa held close to the body.
events.why: Holding a load close to the body squeezed the disc least.

events.title: How muscles grow, reviewed
events.text: Schoenfeld's widely cited review of the mechanisms of muscle hypertrophy weighed mechanical tension, metabolic stress and muscle damage as signals for growth. Later work points to tension as the main one.
events.why: It framed the modern evidence on sets, loads and effort. BicepsClear goes deep on it.

events.title: A state sport
events.text: Madhya Pradesh declared mallakhamb an official state sport.
events.why: Official support keeps a traditional back-and-grip discipline alive for new generations.

events.title: More sets, more growth
events.who: Brad Schoenfeld, Dan Ogborn and James Krieger
events.text: A meta-analysis found that more weekly sets led to more muscle growth. Studies with 10 or more sets per muscle a week did best, though that comparison was only a trend and few studies went higher. A second 2017 meta-analysis found light and heavy loads built similar size when sets went to failure.
events.why: It is the basis for the common '10 or more hard sets a week' advice, stated honestly.

events.title: First World Mallakhamb Championship
events.text: Mumbai hosted the first World Mallakhamb Championship; Himani Uttam Parab won gold in the rope long set.
events.why: A centuries-old Indian back workout became a world sport.

events.title: "Sit up straight" is questioned
events.who: Diane Slater, Peter O'Sullivan and colleagues
events.text: A viewpoint in the Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy argued that there is no single correct posture that protects the back, and that varied, comfortable postures and staying active matter more.
events.why: It challenged a piece of advice almost everyone has heard.

events.title: Fit India is launched
events.text: The Fit India Movement was launched on National Sports Day to encourage everyday physical activity across the country.
events.why: Regular strength and movement are the base for a healthy back.

events.title: To flex or not to flex?
events.who: Nicola Saraceni, Peter O'Sullivan and colleagues
events.text: A systematic review found no clear evidence that bending the lower back while lifting is linked to low back pain. Most of the studies found no difference in lifting flexion between people with and without pain.
events.why: Rounding a little to pick something up is normal; braced neutral is still taught for heavy, repeated lifts.

events.title: WHO: strengthen twice a week
events.text: WHO's 2020 guidelines on physical activity call for muscle-strengthening activities of moderate or greater intensity, working all major muscle groups, on 2 or more days a week.
events.why: The back is one of those major muscle groups.

events.title: Exercise eases chronic back pain
events.text: A Cochrane review found moderate-certainty evidence that exercise reduces chronic low back pain by about 15 points on a 0–100 scale compared with no treatment, usual care or placebo.
events.why: A modest but real effect, with few risks: exercise is treatment.

events.title: WHO's first back pain guideline
events.text: WHO estimated that low back pain affected 619 million people in 2020, rising to a projected 843 million by 2050, and called it the single leading cause of disability worldwide. In December 2023 it released its first guideline on chronic primary low back pain, with structured exercise among the recommended non-surgical care.
events.why: Training the back is now part of how the world's health body says to treat back pain.

events.title: Protein from food, not powders
events.text: The Dietary Guidelines for Indians give about 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight a day for healthy adults and advise against protein supplements for healthy people.
events.why: Dal, milk, curd, eggs, fish and meat spread over the day are enough for most people who train.

facts: In a pull-up you lift all of your body weight; in an inverted row with a level body, about two thirds of it.
Your back muscles pull only about 5.5 cm behind your spine, so in a deadlift they pull many times the weight of the bar.
Holding 20 kg close to the body roughly halved the pressure in one volunteer's lumbar disc compared with lifting it with a round back.
Low back pain is the single leading cause of disability in the world, and exercise is one of the treatments WHO includes.
